papers.title_in_file: Advantage of Quantum Machine Learning from General Computational Advantages
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Formulation, Theorem 1 statement, Discussion and outlook; appendix proofs not read
papers.what_it_is: Theory paper constructing supervised learning tasks (PAC model) with a provable quantum-versus-classical learning separation based on any quantumly advantageous function.

assertions.value: The paper proves that, for any quantumly advantageous function, the constructed concept class is not classically efficiently learnable by any classically efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class, while it is quantumly efficiently learnable.
quotes: CN is not classically efficiently learnable by any classically efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class.
We prove the hardness of achieving this learning task for any possible polynomial-time classical learning method.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 (proof in Methods and Appendix B), main text
assertions.reader_inference: The separation is only as strong as the existence of a quantumly advantageous function; the paper does not exhibit one that is known to exist under standard assumptions beyond the candidates it names.

assertions.value: The authors state that the result applies to a general class of functions that quantum algorithms compute efficiently for a large fraction of inputs and that no classical algorithm computes efficiently.
quotes: for a general class of functions that can be computed efficiently in polynomial time for a large fraction of inputs by quantum algorithms but not by any classical algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its theorem in the Introduction, p.2

assertions.value: The authors propose a protocol for preparing the classical sample data and for estimating classical runtime by extrapolation from small problem sizes; the paper reports no experimental run of it.
quotes: we also propose to perform B's task by only using classical computation for several small problem sizes N
Furthermore, we propose protocols to prepare the classical sample data for the experimental demonstration of this advantage of QML.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposal in the Discussion; no run is reported
assertions.reader_inference: The separation is theoretical; no hardware or simulation result in the sections read.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Resonant Dimensionality Reduction and Its Application in Quantum Machine Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section II complexity comparison, Section III QSVM results, Discussion; QCNN details and appendices skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Proposes a quantum dimensionality reduction algorithm (QRDR) and tests it in classical simulation with a QSVM and a QCNN.

assertions.value: The authors state that QRDR operates with polylogarithmic time complexity and reduces the error dependency, from a higher power of the inverse accuracy to the first power, compared with existing algorithms.
quotes: QRDR operates with polylogarithmic time complexity and reduces the error dependency from the order of
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's own complexity analysis in Section II; the stated comparison holds under assumptions on the reduced dimension and matrix norm given there
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is to QPE-based and QPCA algorithms under the paper's own assumptions.

assertions.value: In a classical simulation on the Sonar mines-versus-rocks dataset, the authors report average QSVM accuracy of 0.8625 on the original data with N = 60 features and 0.8937 after reduction to R = 16.
quotes: Connectionist Bench (Sonar, Mines vs. Rocks) Data Set is used to evaluate our QRDR algorithm.
N = 60 features, the accuracy is 0.8625. For R = 16, the accuracy improves to 0.8937.
assertions.certainty_reason: One small dataset, simulated, averaged over eight cross-validation folds
assertions.reader_inference: One small dataset in simulation; no hardware run and no significance test in the sections read.

assertions.value: The authors evaluate QRDR by numerical simulation and state that large-scale demonstration on NISQ devices still presents challenges.
quotes: We simulate the QRDR algorithm numerically and evaluate its performance using quantum support vector machines
Despite our reduction in quantum resource consumption, achieving large-scale algorithm demonstrations on NISQ
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit in the Discussion

papers.title_in_file: Universal quantum phase classification on quantum computers from machine learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Figure 3 caption, Conclusion and discussion; methods and appendices not read in full
papers.what_it_is: Framework that classifies 1D quantum phases from classical-shadow data using time-series neural networks trained on data from Haar-random finite-depth local unitaries.

assertions.value: The authors report classification accuracy of 0.96 and an AUC of 0.99 on their engineered dataset of Haar-random evolved states.
quotes: On the engineered dataset of Haar-random evolved states, our framework achieves an impressive classification accuracy of 0.96 and an AUC of 0.99
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study, simulated states
assertions.reader_inference: The test set is drawn from the same generator as the training data.

assertions.value: The authors report that the trained model reproduces the phase diagrams and critical points of the Ising and ANNNI models although it was trained on a Hamiltonian-agnostic dataset.
quotes: our model accurately reproduces their intricate phase diagrams and critical points, despite having been trained on a Hamiltonian-agnostic dataset
showing excellent agreement with known phase boundaries.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single study; agreement judged against known phase diagrams

assertions.value: The authors state that training data come from a quantum simulator and that performance under noise and errors in current quantum computers is left to future work.
quotes: In this way, the training data can be efficiently obtained from a quantum simulator.
We will investigate how our model performs under noise and other errors inherent in the current quantum computer in future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit in Section 5
assertions.reader_inference: In the sections read, no run on quantum hardware is reported despite the title.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Annealing for Quantum Chemistry
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section IV results narrative, Section VII Conclusion; appendices not read
papers.what_it_is: Proposes a variational quantum annealing algorithm for molecular electronic structure, tested mostly with simulated annealing and partly on a D-Wave annealer.

assertions.value: The authors report that for H2, He2 and HeH+ the ground and first excited state energies computed with VarQA and the digitizer technique are within chemical accuracy.
quotes: For small molecules, such as H2, He2, and HeH+, the ground and first excited state energies computed using VarQA and the digitizer technique are within chemical accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small molecules, STO-3G basis, mostly simulated annealing
assertions.reader_inference: Applies to the smallest molecules only.

assertions.value: The authors state they evaluated ground-state potential energy surfaces for molecules with up to 20 spin orbitals and one excited-state surface, and that the number of logical qubits equals the number of spin orbitals.
quotes: We demonstrate the effectiveness of VarQA by evaluating the ground-state potential energy surface for molecules with up to 20 spin orbitals as well as an excited-state potential energy surface.
with the number of required logical qubits equal to the number of spin orbitals
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' statement of scope, Abstract

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of limited access to D-Wave QPUs, most calculations used simulated annealing rather than quantum annealing.
quotes: Due to limited access privileges to the D-Wave QPUs, we did not perform QA for all cases. Instead, we performed most of the calculations using Simulated Annealing (SA)
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit in Section IV
assertions.reader_inference: Most reported accuracy therefore does not test quantum annealing hardware.

papers.title_in_file: Non-asymptotic Approximation Error Bounds of Parameterized Quantum Circuits
papers.version_note: File is the NeurIPS 2024 revision (v2) of arXiv 2310.07528, retitled; the filename carries the earlier title. Same paper as the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, theorem statements, Section 5 Discussion; appendix proofs and numerical details not read
papers.what_it_is: Theory paper constructing data re-uploading parameterized quantum circuits and bounding their approximation error for polynomials and smooth functions.

assertions.value: The paper establishes explicit non-asymptotic approximation error bounds for data re-uploading parameterized quantum circuits in terms of qubit count, circuit depth and number of trainable parameters.
quotes: We establish the first non-asymptotic approximation error bounds for these functions in terms of the number of qubits, quantum circuit depth, and number of trainable parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 1 to 4 (Sections 3 and 4); proofs in appendix

assertions.value: The authors state that for functions meeting specific smoothness criteria the circuit size and number of trainable parameters of their PQCs can be smaller than those of deep ReLU neural networks, and that this gap is exponential under the conditions they give.
quotes: the quantum circuit size and number of trainable parameters of our proposed PQCs can be smaller than those of deep ReLU neural networks
is exponentially smaller than the required network size and number of parameters of ReLU FNNs
assertions.certainty_reason: Comparison of upper bounds against a published near-optimal ReLU bound, Section 5 and Appendix E
assertions.reader_inference: This compares model size for approximation only, not training cost, data need or runtime.

assertions.value: The authors state the paper investigates the expressivity of PQCs for approximating multivariate function classes and that they also validate approximation by numerical experiments.
quotes: This paper investigates the expressivity of PQCs for approximating general multivariate function classes.
We further validate the approximation capability of PQCs through numerical experiments.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' statement of scope, Abstract

papers.title_in_file: Does qubit connectivity impact quantum circuit complexity?
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, statements of Theorems 1 to 8; proofs in later sections not read
papers.what_it_is: Circuit-complexity theory paper showing that restricted qubit connectivity does not raise worst-case depth or size beyond a constant factor for almost all unitaries.

assertions.value: The paper proves that any n-qubit unitary can be implemented under one-dimensional chain (path) connectivity with the same asymptotic depth and size as with all-to-all connectivity.
quotes: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented by a quantum circuit of depth O(4n/n) and size O(4n) under path constraint.
Therefore, the above theorem implies that the qubit connectivity constraint does not increase the depth and size complexity (by more than a constant factor) for almost all n-qubit unitaries.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 and the paragraph after it, Introduction
assertions.reader_inference: Asymptotic worst-case result for generic unitaries; hidden constants and specific structured circuits are not covered by the quoted text.

assertions.value: The paper proves that the circuit size for any n-qubit unitary can be kept at the all-to-all order for any connected constraint graph.
quotes: Any n-qubit unitary matrix can be implemented by a quantum circuit of size O(4n) under arbitrary connected graph constraints.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 5

assertions.value: The authors state that with ancilla qubits the circuit depth can be made polynomial, and that the space-depth trade-off is not impaired by connectivity constraints unless exponentially many ancillary qubits are available.
quotes: the space-depth trade-off is not impaired by connectivity constraints unless we have exponentially many ancillary qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 and Abstract

papers.title_in_file: Quantum neural network equipped with backpropagation on a qudit processor
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, experiment and results text, Discussion, baseline comparison paragraph; supplementary noise analysis skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Experiment training a single-qudit quantum neural network on a trapped 40Ca+ ion for a two-class Fashion-MNIST task.

assertions.value: The authors report an experimental test accuracy of 95.7% after 13 training epochs, against 96.7% in numerical simulation with the experimentally trained parameters.
quotes: The network achieved a test accuracy of 95.7% after 13 training epochs, closely matching the numerical simulation (96.7%).
achieve an experimental classification accuracy of 95.7% on a test image set
assertions.certainty_reason: Single hardware experiment

assertions.value: The authors report training on 30 samples (15 T and 15 P) from a two-class Fashion-MNIST task.
quotes: In the experiment, a training set of 30 samples (15 T and 15 P) is used to train our QNN.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' description of their experimental setup

assertions.value: The authors state that a linear support vector machine, a two-qubit QNN and a noise-free simulation reach comparable test performance to the qudit QNN on this small-scale proof-of-principle task.
quotes: We present several baseline comparisons including a linear support vector machine, a two-qubit QNN, and a noise-free numerical simulation
Table I shows that the three models achieve comparable test performance on this small-scale proof-of-principle task.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the baseline paragraph; table values not used here
assertions.reader_inference: The task does not show an advantage of the qudit QNN over a linear SVM or a two-qubit QNN.
